source.title: Decompose Sparsely Where You Should, Absorb Densely Where You Should No
source.authors: Rui-Xuan Deng; Ze-Hao Jin; Ze-Kun Wang; Zi-Han Dong

record.tranche_reason: The paper presents experiments about sparse autoencoders and a low-rank activation component, but does not test neuron-pole job descriptions, explanations against held-out activations, or the other listed claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's measurements concern SAE representations and a proposed computational scaffold, not whether individual neurons or neuron poles have one main job. Its discussion of sparse monosemantic decomposition is related but is not a test of the listed versions. Findings cited from prior work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study measures sparse autoencoder latents and a low-rank residual-stream component in Gemma-2-2B layer 12. It does not audit individual neurons or neuron poles for job shares. It does not analyse InceptionV1, build neuron-based attribution graphs, or score neuron explanations against held-out activations. Its discussion of monosemantic decomposition concerns SAE features, not the essay's neuron claims, and neither original source is cited.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that Gemma-2-2B layer-12 residual streams contain a compact, low-rank 'computational scaffold'. This component is causally critical, semantically informative, aligned with top PCs and outlier dimensions, and represented inefficiently by sparse dictionaries. They argue that sparsity-based interpretability may have a narrower scope than assumed.
record.recipe_differences: The study adds and intervenes on a low-rank linear bottleneck alongside SAEs; it does not explain neuron poles or test explanations on held-out activations.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by SAE architecture for some extraction and intervention metrics; rank and bottleneck linearity also affect outcomes. The study reports only one model and layer.

fits_no_version.finding: A rank-24 linear bottleneck reduced dense SAE latents from 25 to 4 (BatchTopK) and from 69 to 44 (Matryoshka) at Gemma-2-2B layer 12.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A low-rank bottleneck can reduce dense latent counts in residual-stream SAEs in this setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the learned 24-d component raised cross-entropy from 1.90 to 14.3 (BatchTopK) and 13.8 (Matryoshka). Removing the top-24 PCA directions raised it to 5.37, and a random 24-d component had negligible effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The learned low-rank component is causally important for next-token prediction in this model and layer.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating 787 aligned sparse features raised cross-entropy only to 5.5. Bottleneck-dimension ablation sent topic accuracy to chance, while ablating 2,048 sparse atoms left it above 99%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Topic information is compactly held in the bottleneck but redundantly spread across SAE features.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE-latent autointerp scores were .869 vs .857 (BatchTopK) and .865 tied (Matryoshka). Residual dense latents scored .464, and the top-200 features by fire rate scored about .70 (Table 1, Appendix G).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automated interpretability scores of SAE latents are high on average but lower for dense, high-fire-rate latents. This concerns SAE features, not neurons.

record.problems: The experiments use a single model and layer, as the authors acknowledge. The causal intervention protocol uses 200 sequences, but uncertainty estimates for the reported causal effects are not stated. The findings concern SAE representations, not neuron-pole explanations.
record.rows_left_out: Other SAE benchmark metrics and ablations are not included because they do not directly characterize the computational scaffold findings recorded here; see Sections 4.1–4.3 and Appendices A–H.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles and no shares of one-job, two-job or not-understood poles.
No neuron-level job shares in any model. Only one model (Gemma-2-2B) and one layer, using SAE latents.
No analysis of InceptionV1, cat-and-car neurons, pose or recursive generalization.
No estimate of the share of interpretable neurons across tools or architectures.
No attribution graphs from model neurons and no replacement-model comparison.
No test of whether neuron explanations from activating examples predict held-out firing.
Autointerp is reported only for SAE latents, not for neurons. No simulation-based neuron-explanation scores are given and no explainer models are compared.

record.verdict_notes: This is an SAE methods paper. Its residual-stream 'neuron' analysis (Figure 3) ranks dimensions by L2 magnitude and PC loading, not by interpretable job, so it does not bear on V1–V4. The reader's T6 and not-tested statuses are confirmed. 'cites_only' would not fit because neither original is cited; 'discusses' is kept only loosely, for its general discussion of monosemantic decomposition.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or report the claimed shares of one-job, two-job, and not-understood poles.
Does not test neuron-pole job shares across models, architectures, or scale.
Does not analyze the InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not estimate the share of interpretable neurons or test the stated InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
Does not test whether attribution graphs made from a model's own neurons explain behavior without a replacement model.
Does not test whether neuron explanations fit to activating examples predict firing on held-out activations.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B, BatchTopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Added a rank-24 linear bottleneck alongside the SAE.
rows.note: The paper says the count falls sharply; this measures SAE dense latents, not neuron-pole job shares.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B, Matryoshka SAE
rows.operation_detail: Added a rank-24 linear bottleneck alongside the SAE.
rows.note: The paper says the count falls; this measures SAE dense latents, not neuron-pole job shares.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B, BatchTopK SAE bottleneck
rows.operation_detail: Projected out the learned 24-dimensional bottleneck subspace from layer-12 activations.
rows.note: The paper reports a 7.5× increase. The result concerns causal importance of the bottleneck component, not neuron-level interpretability.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B, Matryoshka SAE bottleneck
rows.operation_detail: Projected out the learned 24-dimensional bottleneck subspace from layer-12 activations.
rows.note: The paper reports an effect nearly identical to the BatchTopK bottleneck removal.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.operation_detail: Removed the top-24 PCA directions from layer-12 activations.
rows.note: The paper contrasts this result with removal of the learned bottleneck component.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B
rows.note: The paper describes the effect as negligible but gives no numerical CE value.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B, BatchTopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Ablated the 787 sparse features most aligned with the bottleneck column space.
rows.note: The paper says this was much less than the 14.3 CE after removing the bottleneck component.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B, bottleneck representation
rows.operation_detail: Ablated bottleneck dimensions in descending η² order through K=24.
rows.note: The text says ablation reaches chance by K=24. It does not provide the exact chance accuracy.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B, sparse dictionary
rows.operation_detail: Ablated the top 2,048 sparse atoms ranked by η².
rows.note: The paper contrasts this with bottleneck-dimension ablation.
rows.check: Baseline is given in the text: under the multinomial 57-way protocol the full sparse code scores 99.8%. The baseline should read 99.8%, not 'not stated'.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2B, bottleneck representation
rows.operation_detail: Trained a linear probe on the bottleneck's 24-dimensional latent to predict MMLU subject.

conditions.value: MMLU subject classification, 57 classes, binary OvR

rows.note: The paper compares this with a sparse-code ceiling of 98% under this protocol.
rows.check: The 98% sparse-code ceiling under the same OvR protocol is the natural comparator and could fill the baseline field.
